Galloping across dusty sparse grasslands, the fi ercely territorial tartakka roams in fast moving herds searching for shallow root 
vegetables to dig up with their stout claws. Capable of surviving long months of drought, they are covered in a leathery hide and can 
retain moisture with a thick deposit of fat that runs below their tail. Th ough smaller than the females, the males carelessly ram their 
knobby skulls and reinforced upper humps into each other on a regular basis in a constant reshuffling of herd hierarchy. Th is nearly 
manic behavior works in their favor when they are threatened by predators, both males and females charge forward in a sequence of 
devastating strikes, with long bounding leaps that end in a concussive barrage of meat and bone.

Encountering Witnessing a herd of tartakka on the plains is 
fairly common as they are a rather plentiful, far roaming herd. 
And though each herd only numbers in the dozens, there are a 
multitude that clash for fertile territory. Th ese herbivores often 
react aggressively to any not of their kind, and there is little 
that can calm them once their blood is heated. Alone, a tartakka 
may be more susceptible to handling as it's vulnerable without 
its herd, but getting one alone is often more diffi cult than its 
worth.
